title: The least functional dependence at negative footrule: the lower boundary of the region of Chatterjee's rank correlation and Spearman's footrule
shortTitle: The lower boundary of the Chatterjee–footrule region
oneLine: For every negative footrule, the least possible Chatterjee coefficient, its unique extremal copula and a certificate, completing Rockel's region.
abstract: Chatterjee's rank correlation ξ measures how far one continuous variable is a function of another: 0 under independence, 1 for an exact functional relationship of any shape. Spearman's footrule ψ measures how close the two rankings are: 1 for identical rankings, 0 under independence, down to −1/2. Which pairs (ξ, ψ) can occur together? Rockel determined this exact region except its curved lower edge: for a footrule strictly between −1/2 and 0, the least possible ξ was open. This candidate determines that edge. For every such footrule the least value of ξ is attained by exactly one copula, constructed explicitly: the response takes one of two levels according to whether the predictor's rank lies below a threshold, and the threshold solves a linear integral equation with a triangular kernel. A dual inequality proves optimality over all copulas, and a stability estimate shows that nearly optimal copulas are close to the extremiser. The boundary has an elementary closed form for ψ ≤ −0.4565…, a finite piecewise-elementary evaluation elsewhere and explicit expansions at both ends; for example ξ + 2ψ ≥ −0.6042071… for every copula. Every attainable pair has a radially symmetric representative. Under positive or negative quadrant dependence the full regions are determined; at zero footrule ξ can approach but never reach 1/2 and 3/4 respectively. For stochastically decreasing copulas the lower edge is the same curve and every pair with ξ ≤ −2ψ above it is attained; that ξ ≤ −2ψ is the exact upper edge is stated as a conjecture, not proved. Limits: population coefficients only; closed form only for ψ ≤ −0.4565…, with double-precision values elsewhere; Rockel's earlier family was already numerically close, so the advance is exactness, uniqueness and proof. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 1 (proof): for each k > 0 the copula C_k is the unique minimiser of ξ + 2kψ over all copulas; as k runs from 0 to ∞ these copulas trace the whole open lower edge from independence to the checkerboard, so for every ψ in (−1/2, 0) the least ξ is attained by exactly one copula, which is stochastically decreasing. A stability estimate bounds the distance of any copula from C_k by its excess objective.

Proposition 3 (proof): closed form in hyperbolic functions for ψ ≤ −0.4565437…, a finite piecewise-exponential evaluation otherwise, and the expansions ψ = −√ξ + ξ/4 + O(ξ^{3/2}) near independence and ψ = −1/2 + (1/2 − ξ)² + O((1/2 − ξ)³) near the checkerboard.

Sharp constants (computed from the exact evaluations): ξ + 2ψ ≥ −0.6042071213… for every copula; at ψ = −0.4565437066… the least ξ is 0.3088802920…; the minimum of ξ + ψ is −0.1932281…, against −0.193 for Rockel's best family member. Table 1 lists the least ξ at seven footrule values, e.g. 0.109988 at ψ = −0.3 against Rockel's Jensen bound 0.096731.

Corollary 4, Lemma 5, Theorem 6 and Proposition 7 (proof): every attainable pair has a radially symmetric representative; the full regions under positive and negative quadrant dependence, with zero-footrule sections [0, 1/2) and [0, 3/4), neither endpoint attained.

Proposition 8 (proof) and Conjecture 9 (not proved): for stochastically decreasing copulas ψ ≤ 0 with equality only under independence, the lower edge is the same curve, and every pair between the curve and ξ = −2ψ is attained; ξ ≤ −2ψ as the exact upper edge is a conjecture supported by numerical search.
Theorems 10 and 11 (proof): the construction extends to transport problems with nonuniform margins and to objectives with several absolute-displacement terms.

Credit: the upper edge ψ = √ξ, the corner at ψ = −1/2, the stochastically increasing region, convexity and closedness of the region, attainment of the lower edge by a stochastically decreasing copula, |ψ| ≤ √ξ, the Jensen lower bound and the near-optimal two-parameter family are Rockel's; the radial and quadrant results parallel Orenday Lares and Rockel's for (ξ, β).

narration:
This briefing is about two ways of measuring how two quantities depend on each other.

Chatterjee's coefficient, called xi, asks how far one quantity is determined by the other. It is zero when they are independent, and one when the second is an exact function of the first, whatever the shape of that function. Spearman's footrule asks how close the two rankings are. It is one when the rankings agree, zero under independence, and it can fall to minus one half when the rankings are pushed as far apart as possible.

Which pairs of values can occur together? Marcus Rockel answered most of this question. One curved edge stayed open: when the rankings are pushed apart by a given amount, how small can the functional dependence be?

This paper closes that edge. For every negative footrule above the lowest value, it finds the least possible xi, shows that exactly one joint law of the ranks attains it, and gives a certificate that nothing does better. The extremal law has a simple recipe. The response takes one of two levels, depending on whether the predictor's rank lies below a threshold, and that threshold solves a linear integral equation with a triangular kernel.

One consequence is a sharp inequality. For any pair of continuous quantities, xi plus twice the footrule never falls below about minus zero point six zero four, and that limit cannot be improved. The paper also settles the regions under positive and negative quadrant dependence, and gives a partial answer for stochastically decreasing data, where the last edge is stated as a conjecture rather than a theorem.

There are limits. The results concern population coefficients, not estimates from samples. The closed form covers only the more strongly negative footrules; elsewhere the boundary is a finite numerical calculation, cross-checked but not certified. Rockel's earlier examples were already close, so the advance is exactness, uniqueness and proof.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and computation rather than external peer review, and its paper, code and evidence are linked from the release page.
